To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

globally, each day, there are about 3 million cases of gastrointestinal and respiratory disease caused by bathing/swimming in polluted marine waters and about 12 000 cases of hepatitis A and E caused by eating raw or lightly cooked filter feeding shellfish, with a total health impact estimated to be about one million DALYs per year.

globally, each day, there are some 3.5 million swimmers and bathers who are exposed to polluted sea water containing infectious pathogens, and some 2 million people who eat contaminated filter feeding shell fish, and that this causes some 120 million cases and some 50 million cases respectively of human infectious diseases each year, resulting in about 3 million DALY/year and some 12 billion dollar/year economic losses.

'Wastewater pollution of the sea causes a global health burden of about 3 million disability adjusted life years (DALYs) and an estimated economic loss to the world economy of about 12 billion dollars/year'.
In summary, our research is concerned with
estimating the global burden of diseases caused by pathogenic microorganisms in wastewater discharged into the marine environment.
the global burden of human diseases caused by pathogenic microorganisms carried into the marine environment by wastewater, and the consequent human health effects.
the global health burden of human infectious diseases caused or exacerbated by the sea, i.e. the thalassogenically caused diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the global burden of the thallassogenic diseases is a major global health problem.
the global burden of the thallassogenic diseases human infectious disease caused by wastewater pollution is a major health problem and is a global environmental problem of considerable magnitude.

the global scale of human health effects from the thalassogenesis of human infectious diseases is of major concern to the world's population and that the global health burden of these diseases is a major global public health issue.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the thalassogenics, the human health effects of wastewater pollution of the coastal marine environment, are a global problem, with an annual global health impact of some 3 million disability adjusted life years, with an estimated annual economic impact of some 12 billions dollars.
the thalassogeny hypothesis is a useful conceptual tool for understanding the global scale of the human health impact of wastewater pollution of the world's oceans and seas.

the health burden of thalasso-genic diseases caused by wastewater and human body waste pollution of the seas, is in the same order of magnitude as the health burden of the global burden caused by the major human diseases of malaria and schistosomiasis, which together are estimated to cause 1.3 million deaths per year.
The main takeaway from our work is that
wastewater pollution of coastal waters is a major cause of human infectious disease and is a major global health problem.

the thalassogenics diseases, the human infectious diseases caused or exacerbated by wastewater pollution of coastal waters and by eating shellfish harvested from polluted waters, are a global problem of major proportions.
wastewater pollution of marine coastal waters can result in a global burden of disease which is comparable to the global burden of many other well known infectious diseases.
